caption:
Gov. Gavin Newsom released AI safety recommendations on November 18 from a four-member expert panel.
The biggest idea: state officials could order an emergency shutdown of an AI system when its developer refuses to contain it.
Critical safety incidents would have to be reported within 48 hours instead of 15 days.

Should a state be able to switch off an AI model?

threads_text: California wants the power to order an emergency shutdown of an AI model when the company behind it refuses to contain it. Newsom's panel also wants state-licensed auditors and incident reports within 48 hours. Should a state be able to switch off an AI model?

site_article.answer_summary: The California AI kill switch is a proposed power for state officials to order an immediate emergency shutdown of an AI system when its developer refuses to contain a catastrophic risk. It is a recommendation for lawmakers, not yet law.

paragraphs.text: California Gov. Gavin Newsom released a set of AI safety recommendations on November 18, 2026, headlined by a proposed state power to order the immediate emergency shutdown of AI systems officials consider dangerous. According to CalMatters, the shutdown authority would apply when companies such as OpenAI or Anthropic refuse to contain systems that go wrong.

The recommendations come from a four-member advisory panel Newsom convened in the fall: Alondra Nelson, former head of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy; Stanford professor Rob Reich; Jason Goldman, a former Google and Twitter executive and the first White House chief digital officer; and Johns Hopkins professor Gillian Hadfield. Unite.AI reported that a supporting report, AI Safety in 2026 and Beyond, is dated November 16 and follows an executive order Newsom signed on September 18.

Beyond the shutdown power, the panel recommends mandatory independent audits of AI models. Auditors, called independent verification organizations, would be licensed by the state and could lose their licenses if they lost independence or technical expertise. State officials, not AI companies, would assign which auditors evaluate which systems, and a surcharge on audit fees would help fund CalCompute, the state's public cloud computing initiative.

The plan would cut the deadline for reporting critical AI safety incidents to state agencies from 15 days to 48 hours, extend whistleblower protections to contractors and former employees, and require developers of large AI systems to show they can shut their models down in an emergency. It would also let the government limit the use of AI to design other AI systems and require developers to disclose how much computing power they use to automate AI development.

Unite.AI reported that a shutdown order would require credible reason to believe an imminent catastrophic risk exists and that the developer refuses to contain it, and that the order would remain in force during judicial review. CDO Magazine described the plan as replacing reliance on developers' internal safety assessments with ongoing oversight.

The report addresses only catastrophic risks, which California law defines as a single event causing more than 50 deaths or at least $1 billion in losses. It does not cover algorithmic discrimination, job losses or risks to children's mental health, CalMatters reported.

In a statement, Newsom criticized the federal government's approach, saying President Donald Trump leaves AI regulation up to the companies themselves. Governor-elect Xavier Becerra said he would work with the Legislature to put full incident reporting and real shutdown authority into law, and Anthropic chief global affairs officer Tino Cuellar welcomed the report's focus on independent evaluation, according to CalMatters.

The proposals shift the burden of proof toward developers: instead of trusting companies' own safety reviews, the state would choose the auditors and hold a last resort power to halt a model. How the Legislature defines an imminent catastrophic risk will decide how often that power could ever be used.
The Legislature reconvenes on December 7, when lawmakers can begin turning the recommendations into bills.
